newsitem.title: UK: UK's Exeter Investment exploring OEICs, pensions.
newsitem.headline: UK's Exeter Investment exploring OEICs, pensions.

text.p: Britain's Exeter Investment Group, which announced on Thursday it was to list on the Alternative Investment Market, said it is also ready to develop pension fund business and Open Ended Investment Companies (OEICs).

In an interview, Chief Executive Ian Henderson said the group, which already has expertise in both investment trusts and unit trusts, had been keeping an eye on the development of OEICs, now set for launch in January.
"OEICs span the gap between investment trusts and unit trusts and ease the way for umbrella funds, which is very much in line with our thinking," he said.

Exeter already has a "lifestyle" product which allows retail investors to switch within the group's funds as their investment needs change. Some funds might also be converted into OEIcs, Henderson added.

But he cautioned that UK retail investors were very conservative and there would be no overnight switch to the new fund type. "OEICs are still untried and all sorts of regulatory and legal issues still have to be resolved".
Exeter would not be venturing into Europe with OEICs in the near term, even though the fund type was designed primarily to allow UK-based financial groups to do just that.
"You would need a link with a European institution to do the marketing and we have not pursued that so far," Henderson said.
The group, which comprises Exeter Asset Management Limited, Exeter Fund Managers Ltd and Sinclair Henderson Limited, is also actively considering entering the personal pensions market.

"Both main political parties (Conservative and Labour) have realised they will not be able to keep funding growing pension liabilites from the public purse," said Henderson. "There is a major marketing opportunity in this area and it is good quality business because you can keep a client over 20 or 30 years."

He said asset management firms could rapidly erode the pension market share of Life companies. "We would have a mega-lead over others in this area because of the problem of mis-selling of pensions," he said.
"Investment managers have not yet got a good penetration of this market but there is no doubt that this will evolve in the next five to 10 years," he added.

UK regulators have identified some 500,000 retail investors as having been mis-sold private pensions by commission-driven agents in the 1980s when the British government was encouraging individuals to opt out of state schemes.
Although only 24,000 cases have been documented so far and less than 50 million stg paid out, the eventual bill for redress is estimated at up to 2.0 billion stg.
Henderson said Exeter's admission to AIM and its increased shareholder base would raise the Group's profile with current and potential investors.
"We intend to seek a full listing on the London Stock Exchange within three to four years but at the moment we would not have the critical mass to do that," he said.
Henderson also said he was intending to realise some of his 45 percent stake over the next three years, before retiring.

"I want to reduce my stake significantly but this will be done in a controlled way with the advice of our sponsor (Grieg Middleton & Co)," he said. The group would be looking for a successor and possibly expanding its current five-strong board. Exeter's total funds under management as of October 31, 1996, calculated on a mid-market basis, were 394 million.
